title: Lidar
description: Method of spatial measurement using laser
wiki_lead:
Lidar (, an acronym of light detection and ranging or laser imaging, detection, and ranging, often stylized LiDAR) is a method for determining ranges by targeting an object or a surface with a laser and measuring the time for the reflected light to return to the optical receiver. Lidar may operate in a fixed direction (e.g., vertical) or it may scan directions, in a special combination of 3D scanning and laser scanning.

LiDAR is used within terrestrial, airborne, and mobile equipment around the globe. It is commonly used to make high-resolution maps, with uses in surveying, geodesy, geomatics, archaeology, geography, geology, geomorphology, seismology, forestry, atmospheric physics, and laser guidance. It is used to make digital 3D representations of areas on the Earth's surface and ocean bottom of the intertidal and near coastal zone by varying the wavelength of light. It has also been increasingly used in control and navigation for autonomous cars and for the helicopter Ingenuity on its record-setting flights over the terrain of Mars. Lidar has since been used extensively for atmospheric research and meteorology. Lidar instruments fitted to aircraft and satellites carry out surveying and mapping –  a recent example being the U.S. Geological Survey Experimental Advanced Airborne Research Lidar. NASA has identified lidar as a key technology for enabling autonomous precision safe landing of future robotic and crewed lunar-landing vehicles.

History and etymology
The essential concept of lidar was originated by E. H. Synge in 1930, who envisaged the use of powerful searchlights to probe the atmosphere.
Under the direction of Malcolm Stitch, the Hughes Aircraft Company introduced the first lidar-like system in 1961, shortly after the invention of the laser. Intended for satellite tracking, this system combined laser-focused imaging with the ability to calculate distances by measuring the time for a signal to return using appropriate sensors and data acquisition electronics. It was originally called "Colidar" an acronym for "coherent light detecting and ranging", derived from the term "radar", itself an acronym for "radio detection and ranging". All laser rangefinders, laser altimeters and lidar units are derived from the early colidar systems.
The first practical terrestrial application of a colidar system was the "Colidar Mark II", a large rifle-like laser rangefinder produced in 1963, which had a range of 11 km and an accuracy of 4.5 m, to be used for military targeting. The first mention of lidar as a stand-alone word in 1963 suggests that it originated as a portmanteau of "light" and "radar": "Eventually the laser may provide an extremely sensitive detector of particular wavelengths from distant objects. Meanwhile, it is being used to study the Moon by 'lidar' (light radar) ..."
The name "photonic radar" is sometimes used to mean visible-spectrum range finding like lidar.

grok_lead: LIDAR, an acronym for Light Detection and Ranging, is an active remote sensing technology that uses pulsed laser light to measure distances to targets, enabling the creation of high-resolution, three-dimensional models of surfaces and objects. By emitting rapid laser pulsesâtypically in the near-infrared spectrumâand calculating the time-of-flight for the light to return after reflection, LIDAR systems determine precise ranges, which are combined with positional data from GPS and inertial measurement units (IMUs) to generate georeferenced point clouds of three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z) representing elevation and structure. These point clouds often contain millions to billions of points, resulting in large data volumes ranging from megabytes to terabytes per project, necessitating significant storage, processing power, and compression techniques. This method typically achieves vertical accuracies of 10-30 cm in standard airborne systems, with high-end systems capable of 1-5 cm precision under optimal conditions; however, accuracy can degrade due to hardware quality (scanner, IMU, GNSS calibration), environmental factors (such as fog, rain, and distance-induced angular errors), range, and sensor noise, requiring precise calibration for reliable results. The technology originated in the 1960s, shortly after Theodore Maiman's invention of the first practical laser in 1960, initially as ground-based instruments for atmospheric studies of composition, clouds, and aerosols. Airborne LIDAR emerged in the 1980s with the integration of GPS for georeferencing, achieving decimeter-level precision by the 1990s, and the first commercial systems appeared around 1995, including the SHOALS bathymetric system developed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Over the decades, advancements in laser efficiency, scanning mechanisms, and data processing have expanded its capabilities, with modern systems capable of over 300,000 pulses per second and applications in diverse environments from terrestrial topography to underwater mapping. LIDAR's versatility supports critical applications across multiple fields, including topographic and bathymetric surveying for coastal management and flood risk assessment, as seen in FEMA's post-hurricane mapping efforts. In forestry and ecology, it quantifies canopy structure, tree heights, and biomass for habitat modeling and resource inventory. Atmospheric LIDAR variants profile ozone, aerosols, and wind patterns from ground or space-based platforms, aiding climate research. Additionally, ground-based and mobile LIDAR facilitates infrastructure mapping for transportation planning and energy siting, while emerging uses in precision agriculture measure crop structure and terrain for optimized farming. LiDAR also serves as a core sensor in robotics for precise 3D environmental perception, enabling simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), navigation, obstacle avoidance, real-time mapping, path planning in dynamic environments, object detection, and sensor fusion with cameras and radar for robust performance across varied lighting and weather conditions. It outperforms camera-based systems in accurate depth perception and reliability under diverse conditions. Key applications include warehouse and manufacturing automation with autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and automated guided vehicles (AGVs), service robots such as vacuum cleaners and lawn mowers, assistive devices including power wheelchairs, agriculture, security, and emerging humanoid robots. Examples include LiDAR-equipped robot lawn mowers (with global shipments of robotic lawn mowers reaching millions of units in 2025 for outdoor mapping and obstacle avoidance), Dreame's robotic vacuums and lawn mowers, the Strutt EV1 assistive wheelchair using LiDAR for collision avoidance and shared control navigation, Hesai's JT series LiDAR in mobile robots, companion robots, and drone delivery systems (e.g., Meituan's Keeta Drone), and warehouse AMRs for material handling. As of early 2026, trends include increasingly affordable solid-state LiDAR (around $400â500 per unit), AI integration for edge processing and real-time intelligence, miniaturization for smaller robots, and expansion into physical AI and humanoids. As of the end of fiscal year 2024, baseline LIDAR data is available or in progress for approximately 98% of the U.S., underscoring its role in environmental monitoring and disaster response.
